analysis.one_liner: Restores OSHA's authority to cite employers for unrecorded workplace injuries, reversing a 2017 repeal.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote: it sat in the House Education and Labor Committee from its introduction in February 2021 until the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the OSH Act, OSHA generally has only six months from a violation to cite an employer, and in 2017 Congress used the Congressional Review Act to strike down an OSHA rule that said an employer's duty to keep accurate injury and illness records is ongoing. This bill would make the six-month clock start only after a continuing violation ends, and would direct OSHA to reissue the recordkeeping rule so employers could not escape responsibility simply because they failed to create injury records in the first place. It died in committee without any action.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at employers who keep inaccurate or missing injury and illness records. OSHA currently may be barred from citing a violation because more than six months passed, even though the violation continues, and employers whose records were never accurate in the first place can escape the recordkeeping duty. The bill extends enforcement in both situations, giving OSHA more time to act and restoring the ongoing duty to maintain accurate records.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers covered by OSHA safety rules

how_it_helps.text: For violations that occur over a period of time, the six-month citation window would not begin until the violation ends, allowing OSHA to cite employers for continuing safety violations [S2] [S3].

The bill would require OSHA to issue a rule clarifying that the duty to make and maintain accurate injury and illness records is ongoing, lasts as long as the record-retention period (typically five years), and does not expire because an employer failed to create the records when first required [S2] [S3].
Congress nullified a nearly identical recordkeeping rule on April 3, 2017, so this bill would restore a protection that was struck down [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers covered by OSHA recordkeeping and citation rules, who would face a longer window for citations and a restored ongoing duty to keep accurate injury and illness records, with the associated costs of compliance and of potential penalties for violations.

drawbacks.text: Extending the six-month citation clock indefinitely for continuing violations could expose employers to citations for conditions that predate an inspection by years, including conditions that changed hands with a business, which employer groups consider unfair when OSHA could have inspected at any time (a general objection to open-ended enforcement periods; not addressed in the provided sources).

The bill gives OSHA 180 days to issue a final rule, a timeline critics of expedited rulemaking argue leaves too little room for public comment and economic analysis (a general objection; the text sets the deadline without a comment schedule) [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is narrow and targeted: it restores a recordkeeping rule Congress struck down in 2017 and fixes the citation clock for continuing violations. The benefit to workers is better enforcement against employers whose injury records are missing or false, which also makes the national injury data more accurate. The cost falls on covered employers in the form of compliance and enforcement exposure. The main design question is how far the extended citation window reaches, which the bill resolves expansively.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee the day it was introduced and never received any further action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 18, 2021 by Rep. Mark Takano with four original cosponsors [S1] [S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor on the day of introduction, and no hearing, markup, or floor action followed during the 117th Congress [S1] [S5].
The bill had 5 cosponsors, all Democrats [S4].

The bill's changes respond to two limits on OSHA enforcement: the six-month statute of limitations for citations, and the 2017 nullification by Congress of a rule making recordkeeping an ongoing obligation [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers subject to OSHA recordkeeping and citation rules are better off because the bill died: they keep the six-month citation clock as written and face no restored ongoing duty to maintain accurate injury records. OSHA's enforcement authority over missing or false injury records remains as narrowed by the 2017 nullification.

for.name: Mark Takano
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to restore OSHA's citation and recordkeeping authority.

sides.party_line_note: All six supporters, including the sponsor and 5 cosponsors, were House Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-chaired committee took no action [S4] [S5].

industries.industry: Employers covered by OSHA recordkeeping rules
industries.note: The bill would lengthen the window for citations of continuing violations and restore an ongoing duty to keep accurate injury and illness records, increasing compliance and enforcement exposure. Its failure preserves the status quo in which missing records can end the enforcement obligation.

industries.industry: Occupational safety compliance and recordkeeping services
industries.note: Restored ongoing recordkeeping duties and stricter citation rules would increase demand for workplace safety compliance and auditing services, whose work also makes injury data more accurate.
